stem: Before feeding text into a language model, it must be broken into smaller pieces called tokens. Which basic Python string operation is conceptually closest to a simple, naive word-level tokenizer?
explanation_after: `.split()` breaks a string into a list of pieces on whitespace — the same core idea behind tokenization: breaking continuous text into discrete units a model can process. Real tokenizers used by models like GPT are more sophisticated (they split on subwords using algorithms like byte-pair encoding, not just whitespace), but the underlying goal is identical: turn one long string into a sequence of smaller pieces.

stem: Why is repeatedly concatenating strings in a loop (e.g., `result = result + next_word` thousands of times) considered inefficient in Python, making `''.join(list_of_words)` the preferred approach for building large text datasets?

options.text: Because strings are immutable — each concatenation creates an entirely new string in memory, copying all previous characters again, which gets slower as the string grows
Because Python doesn't allow the `+` operator to be used on strings
Because loops are not allowed to contain string operations
Because `+` only works correctly on numbers, not text

explanation_after: Because strings can't be changed in place, `result + next_word` builds a brand-new string every single time, re-copying everything accumulated so far. Over thousands of iterations this becomes quadratically slow. `''.join()` instead builds the final string once from a list, which is why it's the standard approach when assembling large text datasets for NLP preprocessing.
